p.src: Now Xue Ba raised his cudgel in both hands and brought it down upon Lin Chong's head. But even as Xue Ba raised his cudgel, swift as lightning there came a thunderous roar from behind a pine, and an iron monk's staff flew out, struck the cudgel aside, and sent it hurtling beyond the clouds. Out leapt a huge, burly monk, shouting, “I've been listening to you scoundrels in these woods for a long while!” When the two escorts looked at the monk, they saw him dressed in a black cloth robe, a monastic sword at his waist. He seized his staff, swung it round, and made to strike them.

p.src: Only then did Lin Chong open his eyes and look; he recognized Lu Zhishen. Lin Chong hastily cried, “Brother, do not strike! I have something to say.” Hearing this, Zhishen checked his staff. The two escorts stood dazed for a long while, unable to move. Lin Chong said, “The fault is not theirs. Grand Marshal Gao had Constable Lu order these two escorts to take my life. How could they refuse him? If you kill them, they too will have died unjustly.”

p.src: Lu Zhishen drew his monastic sword and cut through all the ropes. Helping Lin Chong to his feet, he said, “Brother, ever since we parted on the day I went with you to buy that sword, I have been deeply worried for you. When you became entangled in the case, I had no way to rescue you. I learned that you had been sentenced to exile in Cangzhou, but could not find you outside the Kaifeng prefectural offices. Then I heard that you were being held in the guards' quarters, and saw an inn servant come to summon the two escorts, saying, ‘A gentleman at the inn wishes to speak with you.’ That made me suspicious, and I could not set my mind at ease about you. Fearing these rogues would harm you on the road, I followed you especially. When I saw these two wretches take you into the inn, I lodged there as well. During the night, I heard the two rogues plotting and tricking you into scalding your feet with boiling water. I wanted to kill the two wretches then and there, but the inn was crowded, and I feared someone might come to their aid. Seeing that they meant you no good, I became still more unable to leave you. When you set out at the fifth watch, I came ahead to these woods to wait and kill the two wretches. They came here to murder you, giving me the perfect chance to kill them.” Lin Chong urged him, “Since you have saved me, brother, please do not take their lives.” Lu Zhishen roared, “You two wretches! Were it not for my brother's sake, I would hack the pair of you into meat paste! For his sake alone, I will spare your lives.” He sheathed his sword there and shouted, “You two wretches, hurry and support my brother. All of you, follow me!” Staff in hand, he strode ahead. The two escorts dared not answer back and could only plead, “Instructor Lin, save us!” They put their bundles back on their shoulders, picked up their cudgels, and supported Lin Chong. They also carried his bundle for him, and all together followed Zhishen out of the woods. After traveling three or four li, they saw a small tavern at the entrance to a village, and the four went in and sat down. And when one looked upon the tavern, this is what appeared:

p.src: Before it ran the post road; behind it lay a streamside village. Several peach and willow trees spread dense green shade; here and there sunflowers and pomegranates tossed their crimson hues. Beyond the door, hemp and wheat grew thick; before the window, lotus blossoms flourished. A light wine banner danced in the fragrant breeze; a short reed blind screened out the scorching sun. By the wall stood earthen jars, brimming clear and cool with country wine; on the shelves were porcelain bottles, newly opened festival brew wafting sweet fragrance. A white-haired old farmer washed the vessels himself, while a rosy-cheeked village girl smiled behind the wine counter.

p.src: Zhishen, Lin Chong, Dong Chao, and Xue Ba now sat down in the village tavern. They called the servant and ordered five or seven jin of meat and two flagons of wine, then had him knead some flour into flatbreads. The servant prepared everything while warming and serving the wine. The two escorts said, “May we respectfully ask at which monastery you reside, Master?” Zhishen laughed. “Why do you two wretches ask where I live? Do you mean to tell Gao Qiu so that he can contrive some way to deal with me? Others may fear him, but I do not. If I ever run into that scoundrel, I shall give him three hundred strokes of my staff!” The two escorts dared not say another word. After eating some wine and meat, they gathered their baggage, paid the bill, and left the village tavern. Lin Chong asked, “Brother, where are you bound now?” Lu Zhishen replied, “If you kill a man, you must see his blood; if you save a man, you must save him to the end. I cannot leave you to your fate; I shall escort you all the way to Cangzhou.” Hearing this, the two escorts secretly lamented, “This is bitter indeed! He has ruined our undertaking. When we return, what can we possibly report? For now, we can only submit to him and travel on together.” A poem bears witness:

p.src: Most hateful are wicked schemes that deceive broad daylight; alone he upholds honor, holding gold in contempt. He fears not a thousand stages of the distant road; through every hardship, one loyal heart endures.

p.src: From then on, Lu Zhishen decided when they traveled and when they rested; how could the escorts dare oppose him? When pleased, he cursed them; when displeased, he struck them. The two escorts dared not raise their voices, fearing the monk would erupt in fury. After two stages, they hired a cart. Lin Chong rode in it to recuperate, while the other three walked alongside. The two escorts harbored anxious thoughts, each concerned only with saving his own life, and had no choice but to proceed cautiously and obediently. All along the road, Lu Zhishen bought wine and meat to nurse Lin Chong, and the two escorts ate as well. Whenever they came to an inn, they rested early and set out late; the two escorts always had to light the fire and cook. Who would dare disobey him? The two secretly conferred: “This monk has taken complete charge of us. When we return, Grand Marshal Gao will surely punish us.” Xue Ba said, “I have heard that a new monk named Lu Zhishen recently came to the vegetable garden quarters of the Great Xiangguo Monastery. This must surely be he. When we return, we shall tell the truth: we meant to finish Lin Chong off in Wild Boar Forest, but this monk rescued him and escorted him all the way to Cangzhou, so we had no chance to act. At worst, we shall return his ten taels of gold and let Lu Qian seek out this monk himself. You and I need only keep ourselves clear of the matter.” Dong Chao said, “That is well said.” The two settled the matter in secret, and nothing more need be said of it.

p.src: But let us leave needless details aside. With Zhishen watching over them without ever leaving their side, they traveled for seventeen or eighteen days, until Cangzhou lay only some seventy li ahead. From there onward, homes stood all along the road, and there were no more lonely places. Once Lu Zhishen had made certain of this, he stopped for a short rest in a pine grove. Zhishen said to Lin Chong, “Brother, Cangzhou is not far from here. There are homes all along the road ahead and no secluded spots anywhere; I have made certain of it. Now you and I must part; may we meet again someday.” Lin Chong said, “When you return, Elder Brother, please tell my father-in-law what has happened. If I survive, I shall richly repay your protection.” Lu Zhishen took out another ten or twenty taels of silver for Lin Chong, then gave two or three taels to the two escorts and said, “You two wretches! I ought to have cut off both your heads on the road, but for my brother’s sake I spared your miserable lives. There is not much road left now, so harbor no wicked designs.” The two replied, “How would we dare do so again? It was all done at the grand marshal’s command.” They accepted the silver and were about to part when Lu Zhishen looked at the escorts and said, “Are the heads of you two wretches as hard as this pine tree?” They answered, “Our heads are but flesh from our parents wrapped around a few bones.” Zhishen swung his monk’s staff and struck the pine just once, leaving a mark two inches deep and snapping the trunk clean through. He roared, “If either of you wretches conceives an evil thought, I shall make your heads end like this tree!” Waving his hand, he dragged away his monk’s staff and called, “Take care, brother.” Then he went back alone. Dong Chao and Xue Ba stuck out their tongues in amazement and could not draw them back for a long while. Lin Chong said, “Sirs, let us be on our way.” The two escorts said, “What a fierce monk! He broke a whole tree with one blow.” Lin Chong said, “That is nothing. At the Xiangguo Temple, he once pulled up a willow tree by the roots.” The two men could only shake their heads; only then did they realize that the tale was true.

p.src: The three left the pine grove and traveled until noon, when they soon caught sight of an inn beside the highway. This is what they saw:

This is what they saw:

p.src: An ancient road, a lonely village, an inn beside the way. By the willow-lined bank, brocade banners droop in the dawn; over the lotus pond, the wind stirs the green wine banner. Liu Ling lies supine before the painted couch; Li Bai sleeps drunk upon the pictured wall. Village brew gives courage to the farmer; rustic wine lends cheer to the old countryman. Immortals have left their jade pendants here; even ministers and lords must pawn their golden sable ornaments.

p.src: The three entered the inn, and Lin Chong invited the two escorts to take the seats of honor. Only after a long while did Dong and Xue begin to feel at ease. There were several tables in the inn, and three or five serving boys were all in a frantic bustle, carrying things to and fro. Lin Chong and the two escorts sat for half an hour, yet no server came to attend them. At last Lin Chong lost patience, rapped on the table, and said, “Your establishment treats its guests shamefully! Because you see I am a prisoner, you will not attend me. Surely I do not mean to eat without paying—what sense is there in this?” The innkeeper said, “So you do not understand that I meant you well.” Lin Chong said, “What kindness is there in refusing to sell me wine and meat?” The innkeeper replied, “You do not know that a wealthy gentleman in this village is named Chai Jin. Here he is called Lord Chai, while throughout the rivers and lakes men call him the ‘Little Whirlwind.’ He is a descendant of Emperor Shizong of the Later Zhou. Since his house yielded the throne at Chenqiao, Emperor Taizu, the Martial-Virtued Emperor, bestowed upon the family a sworn covenant and iron certificate. Who would dare mistreat him? He makes a special practice of welcoming worthy men who travel the realm, keeping thirty or fifty of them in his household. He often instructs us innkeepers, ‘If any exiled prisoner comes by, send him to my manor, and I shall provide for him myself.’ If I sell you wine and meat now and you arrive with a ruddy face from eating and drinking, he will think you have traveling money of your own and give you no aid. I acted only out of kindness.” Hearing this, Lin Chong said to the two escorts, “When I served as an arms instructor in the Eastern Capital, I often heard soldiers speak of Lord Chai. So this is where he lives. Why should we not go together and seek his protection?” Dong Chao and Xue Ba thought, “If that is so, what have we to lose?” They immediately gathered their bundles and, together with Lin Chong, asked, “Innkeeper, where is Lord Chai’s manor? We are just setting out to find him.” The innkeeper said, “It lies straight ahead, perhaps two or three li away. Turn around the bend beside the great stone bridge, and the large manor you see will be his.”

Beyond the bridge stretched a broad, level road, and soon they saw the manor emerging from the shade of green willows. A stream encircled the place on every side; great weeping willows lined both banks, and within their shade ran a whitewashed wall. They rounded the bend and reached the front. What a magnificent manor it was! This is what they saw:

p.src: Its gate faced the auspicious way; its hills joined the Azure Dragon. Ten thousand peach boughs bloomed by Wuling Stream; a thousand flowering trees opened in Golden Valley Garden. In the Hall for Gathering Worthies, wondrous blossoms never faded throughout the four seasons; before the Hall of a Hundred Flowers, every season rivaled the beauty of eternal spring. An imperial golden plaque hung in the hall, and the house possessed a sworn covenant and iron certificate. Vermilion eaves and emerald tiles set off nine tiers of lofty halls; painted rafters and carved beams made it truly a residence of the highest refinement. If this was not the mansion of an honored kinsman of the present court, it must surely have been the palace of an emperor of old.

p.src: The three reached the manor and saw four or five retainers sitting on the broad plank bridge, enjoying the cool air. They approached the bridge and saluted the retainers, whereupon Lin Chong said, “Please, good sirs, report to your lord that a prisoner from the capital, surnamed Lin and being escorted to a prison fortress, begs an audience.” The retainers all said, “You are out of luck. If our lord were home, he would give you food, wine, and money, but he went hunting early this morning.” Lin Chong asked, “Do you know when he will return?” A retainer replied, “There is no telling. He may well go to the eastern manor and stay there. We cannot promise you anything.” Lin Chong said, “Then it is my misfortune that I cannot meet him. Let us go.” Taking leave of the retainers, he returned along the old road with the two escorts, deeply troubled at heart.

p.src: Every man was handsome and imposing; each one bore the air of a hero. Dozens of fine horses neighed into the wind, while two or three embroidered banners played in the sunlight. Their pale blue felt hats were held high like upturned lotus leaves; their crimson tassels looked like brilliant lotus blossoms thrust in profusion. In their flying-fish bow cases stood slender, finely painted bows adorned with golden sparrows; in their lion quivers were neatly gathered straight arrows with kingfisher ornaments and eagle-feather fletching. They led several slender hounds for chasing roe deer and carried several pairs of goshawks for taking rabbits. Handsome falcons that pierced the clouds tugged against their silken jesses; hooded brocade-plumed eagles sought the falconer’s glove. Sharp javelins beside the saddles revealed a faint, cold gleam; round painted drums upon the horses thundered from time to time. Everything tied beside the saddles was a bird that had flown beyond the skies; everything borne aloft on horseback was a beast that had roamed the mountains. They seemed like the Prince of Jin approaching the Purple Frontier, or Emperor Wu of Han arriving at the Changyang Palace.

p.src: That company of horsemen came galloping toward the manor, clustered around a gentleman mounted on a snow-white, curly-haired horse. The rider had arched brows and phoenix eyes, gleaming teeth and vermilion lips, with a trim three-pointed mustache and beard about his mouth, and was some thirty-four or thirty-five years old. On his head he wore a black gauze kerchief with upturned corners and clustered flowers; on his body, a purple embroidered robe with a round floral breast panel; around his waist, an exquisitely worked cord set with jeweled jade rings; and on his feet, black court boots with green trim and gold stitching. Carrying a bow and a quiver of arrows, he led his attendants up to the manor. At the sight of him, Lin Chong wondered, “Could this be the nobleman Chai?” Yet he dared not ask and merely hesitated inwardly. Then the young gentleman on horseback spurred forward and asked, “Who is this man wearing a cangue?” Lin Chong hurriedly bowed and replied, “I am Lin Chong, formerly an arms instructor of the Imperial Guards in the Eastern Capital. Because I offended Grand Marshal Gao, he contrived a charge against me and had me sent before the Kaifeng prefecture. I was convicted, sentenced, tattooed, and banished here to Cangzhou. At an inn up ahead, I heard that the nobleman Chai, a hero who welcomes worthy and talented men, lived here, and so I came especially to seek his protection. But alas, my affinity with him must be too slight, for I have failed to meet him.” The gentleman swung himself from the saddle, hastened forward, and said, “I, Chai Jin, have failed to come out and welcome you.” There on the grass, he bowed at once. Lin Chong hurriedly returned the courtesy. The gentleman took Lin Chong by the hand, and together they walked to the manor. When the manor servants saw them, they threw the gates wide open, and Chai Jin invited Lin Chong straight into the front hall. After they had exchanged formal courtesies, Chai Jin said, “I have long heard of your great name, Instructor. I never expected you to honor my humble estate today; thus is fulfilled the lifelong wish born of my admiration for you.” Lin Chong replied, “I am but the lowly Lin Chong. Your honored name, sir, is renowned throughout the realm—who does not revere you? Never did I imagine that, having been convicted and banished here, I should behold your honored countenance. It is the greatest blessing of my life.” After repeatedly yielding precedence, Chai Jin had Lin Chong take the guest seat. Dong Chao and Xue Ba were seated along with him. Chai Jin’s attendants each led away a horse to rest in the rear courtyard, and there is no more to tell of that.

p.src: Chai Jin summoned the manor servants and told them to bring wine. Before long, several servants brought out a platter of meat and a platter of cakes, and warmed a flask of wine. Another brought a tray holding a dou of white rice with ten strings of cash laid upon it; all were presented together. Seeing this, Chai Jin said, “These country louts have no sense of propriety! How can they treat the Instructor so slightingly when he has come here? Take these away at once. First bring fruit boxes and wine, then slaughter a sheep to entertain our guest. Go and prepare it quickly!” Lin Chong rose and thanked him. “My lord, there is no need to bestow so much. This is already more than enough.” Chai Jin said, “Do not speak so. It is a rare honor to have you here, Instructor. How could I possibly treat you with neglect?” The servants dared not disobey and first brought out the fruit boxes and wine. Chai Jin rose and personally offered three cups in succession. Lin Chong thanked Chai Jin and drank; afterward the two constables drank as well. Chai Jin said, “Instructor, please come inside and sit awhile.” Chai Jin then removed his bow case and quiver and invited the two constables to drink with them.

p.src: Chai Jin took the host’s place, Lin Chong the guest’s, and the two constables sat below Lin Chong. As they chatted of various matters and affairs of the rivers and lakes, the red sun sank in the west before they knew it. Wine, food, fruit, and delicacies from the sea were prepared, set upon tables, and carried before each man. Chai Jin personally raised his cup and led three rounds of drinking. Then he sat down and called, “Bring the soup, and let us eat.” They had taken one course of soup and five or seven cups of wine when a servant came to report, “The arms master has arrived.” Chai Jin said, “Invite him in. It will be good for everyone to sit together and meet. Quickly bring another table.” Lin Chong rose to look and saw the arms master enter the rear hall, his headcloth cocked to one side and his chest thrust out. Lin Chong thought, “Since the servants call him ‘Master,’ he must be my lord’s own teacher.” He hurriedly bowed and offered a formal greeting. “Lin Chong respectfully pays his respects.” The man paid him no attention at all and did not return the greeting. Lin Chong dared not raise his head. Chai Jin pointed to Lin Chong and said to Instructor Hong, “This is none other than Lin Chong, Master Lin, the spear-and-staff instructor of the eight hundred thousand Imperial Guards in the Eastern Capital. You two should meet.” Hearing this, Lin Chong turned to Instructor Hong and bowed. Instructor Hong said, “No need to bow. Get up.” But he did not bend to return the courtesy. Seeing this, Chai Jin was deeply displeased. Lin Chong bowed twice, then rose and offered Instructor Hong a seat. Instructor Hong made no show of yielding precedence but went straight to the place of honor and sat down. Chai Jin saw this and was displeased again. Lin Chong had no choice but to sit below him, and the two constables also took their seats.

p.src: Instructor Hong asked, “My lord, why are you treating a banished prisoner so lavishly today?” Chai Jin said, “This man is not like the others. He was an instructor of the eight hundred thousand Imperial Guards. How can you slight him, Master?” Instructor Hong said, “My lord, merely because you are fond of practicing spear and staff, banished prisoners often come here claiming connections and seeking patronage. They all say, ‘I am a spear-and-staff instructor,’ and seek shelter at your manor to wheedle wine, food, money, and rice from you. Why do you take them so seriously, my lord?” Lin Chong heard him but said nothing. Chai Jin said, “A man must not be judged lightly. Do not underestimate him.” Instructor Hong took offense at Chai Jin’s words, “Do not underestimate him.” He sprang to his feet and said, “I do not believe in him. If he dares exchange a bout with me using staffs, then I will admit he is a true instructor.” Chai Jin laughed heartily. “Excellent! Excellent! Master Lin, what do you say?” Lin Chong said, “I would not dare.” Instructor Hong thought, “The fellow surely has no skill and has already lost his nerve.” And so he pressed Lin Chong all the more to take up a staff. For one thing, Chai Jin wanted to see Lin Chong’s true ability. For another, he wanted Lin Chong to defeat Hong and silence the fellow’s boasting. Chai Jin said, “Let us drink for now. We can wait until the moon rises.”

p.src: The two instructors exchanged four or five rounds beneath the bright moon, when suddenly Lin Chong sprang out of the ring and called, “Rest a moment.” Chai Jin asked, “Instructor, why do you not use your true skill?” Lin Chong said, “I have lost.” Chai Jin said, “We have not yet seen you two properly matched. How can you already have lost?” Lin Chong replied, “I alone am burdened with this cangue, so for that reason I shall count myself defeated.” Chai Jin said, “It was thoughtless of me not to consider that.” Laughing heartily, he added, “That is easily remedied.” He ordered a manor servant to fetch ten taels of silver, which was brought at once. Chai Jin addressed the two constables escorting the prisoner: “I venture to trouble you both to condescend to remove Instructor Lin’s cangue for the moment. If any difficulty arises at the prison camp tomorrow, I shall bear full responsibility. Here are ten taels of silver for you.” Dong Chao and Xue Ba saw that Chai Jin was a man of imposing presence and dared not oppose him. They could do him a favor and gain ten taels of silver besides, nor did they fear Lin Chong would escape. Xue Ba immediately removed the cangue from Lin Chong’s neck. Greatly delighted, Chai Jin said, “Now let the two instructors try another bout.”

p.src: Having seen Lin Chong’s timid staffwork just before, Instructor Hong privately despised him and raised his staff, ready to begin. Chai Jin called out, “Wait!” He ordered a manor servant to bring out a silver ingot weighing twenty-five taels. In no time it was brought before him. Chai Jin then said, “This contest between you two instructors is no ordinary match. Let this ingot of silver serve for the moment as the prize. Whoever wins shall take this silver away.” Chai Jin only wanted Lin Chong to display his true skill, so he deliberately tossed the silver onto the ground. Instructor Hong bitterly resented Lin Chong; he also coveted the large silver ingot and feared losing his prestige. He wielded his staff with all his might, displayed an opening posture, and assumed the stance known as “Holding the Torch to Burn the Sky.” Lin Chong thought, “In his heart, Master Chai wants only for me to defeat him.” He too held his staff crosswise, displayed an opening, and assumed a stance called “Parting the Grass to Seek the Snake.” Instructor Hong shouted, “Come, come, come!” Then he brought his staff crashing down upon him. Lin Chong retreated a step. Instructor Hong pressed forward one step, raised his staff, and struck down once more. Lin Chong saw that his footwork was already disordered. He flicked his staff upward from near the ground, catching Instructor Hong unprepared; in that same upward stroke he turned his whole body, and the staff swept squarely into Hong’s shinbone. Hong dropped his staff and fell flat to the ground. Chai Jin was overjoyed and called for wine to be brought quickly so that he might offer a cup. Everyone burst into laughter together. Instructor Hong struggled to his feet. The manor servants, laughing all the while, helped Instructor Hong up. His face covered with shame, he went off by himself beyond the manor grounds.

p.src: Chai Jin kept Lin Chong at his manor for several days in succession, treating him each day to fine wine and good food. Chai Jin once more prepared a banquet to entertain them and see them on their way; He also wrote two letters and instructed Lin Chong: “The governor of Cangzhou is on good terms with me, and the superintendent and the warder of the prison camp are likewise close friends of mine. p.src: The three took the road toward Cangzhou. By around noon they had entered the city. Though it was a small place, it still had its busy streets and marketplaces. They went straight to the prefectural yamen and delivered the official papers. Lin Chong was brought before the prefect in the main hall. The authorities took him into custody, endorsed the return document, issued the necessary posting, and sentenced him to be conveyed to the prison camp. The two constables collected the return document, took their leave, and went back to the Eastern Capital. Of them, no more need be said.

p.src: At the Cangzhou prison camp, Lin Chong was taken into custody and placed in the newcomers’ quarters to await inspection. The other prisoners came to see him and told him, “The commandant and the warder here are vicious men whose sole aim is to extort money and goods from people. If you give them money or gifts to win their favor, they will treat you well; but if you have no money, they will cast you into an underground cell, where you can neither live nor die. If you have secured their favor, they will spare you the hundred initiation strokes when you enter, merely saying you are ill and postponing them; but if you have not, those hundred strokes will leave you more dead than alive.” Lin Chong said, “Thank you, brothers, for telling me this. If money must be spent, how much should I give them?” They replied, “If you want everything handled properly, give the commandant five taels of silver and the warder another five. That will settle matters splendidly.”

but if you have not, those hundred strokes will leave you more dead than alive.”
Lin Chong said, “Thank you, brothers, for telling me this. If money must be spent, how much should I give them?”
They replied, “If you want everything handled properly, give the commandant five taels of silver and the warder another five. That will settle matters splendidly.”

p.src: While they were speaking, the warder came over and demanded, “Which one is the newly arrived convict?” Hearing the question, Lin Chong stepped forward and answered, “I am, sir.” Seeing that he produced no money, the warder’s expression changed. Pointing at Lin Chong, he cursed, “You thieving convict! Why did you not prostrate yourself when you saw me? You merely offer a standing salute! No wonder you got into trouble in the Eastern Capital—you still swagger before me as brazenly as ever. This thieving convict has the look of starvation written all over his face; he will never prosper as long as he lives! You incorrigible wretch whom neither beating nor torture can kill! Now that your thieving carcass has fallen into my hands, one way or another I shall grind your bones to dust. Before long, I shall show you what I can do.” The torrent of abuse left Lin Chong utterly confounded; he dared neither raise his head nor answer. At the sight of this abuse, the others dispersed.

p.src: After Lin Chong had let him vent his fury, he fetched five taels of silver and, smiling ingratiatingly, said, “Brother Warder, here is a trifling gift. Please do not think it too slight.” The warder looked at it and asked, “Does this include what I am to give the commandant as well as my own share?” Lin Chong replied, “This is only for you, Brother Warder; I have another ten taels of silver, which I shall trouble you to deliver to the commandant.” At this, the warder looked at Lin Chong and smiled. “Arms Instructor Lin, I too have heard of your fine reputation. You are truly a splendid man! I suppose Grand Marshal Gao framed you. Though you must suffer for a while at present, in time you are certain to rise in the world. With your great name and imposing appearance, you cannot be an ordinary man; one day you are sure to become a high official.” Lin Chong smiled and said, “I shall depend entirely upon your care.” The warder said, “You may set your mind at ease.” Lin Chong then took out Lord Chai’s letters and gifts and said, “May I trouble you, brother, to deliver these two letters?” The warder replied, “If you have letters from Lord Chai, what is there to worry about? One such letter is worth an ingot of gold. I shall deliver the letters for you at once. When the commandant comes shortly to inspect you and orders the hundred initiation strokes, simply say, ‘I fell ill along the road and have not yet recovered.’ I shall speak up for you and make a show of things for the benefit of the strangers watching.” Lin Chong said, “Many thanks for your guidance.” Taking the silver and the letters, the warder left the newcomers’ quarters and went his way. Lin Chong sighed and said, “‘Money can move even the gods’—the saying is indeed true. Such are truly the hardships of this place.”

p.src: As it happened, the warder kept five taels of silver for himself and took only five taels and the letters to the commandant. He explained in detail that Lin Chong was a fine man and that Lord Chai had written to recommend him, then presented the letters. He had been framed by Grand Marshal Gao and banished here, although he had committed no very serious offense. The commandant said, “Since Lord Chai has written on his behalf, we must be sure to look after him.” He then ordered Lin Chong to be summoned before him.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lin Chong was sitting dejectedly in the newcomers’ quarters when he heard a squad leader call, “The commandant is in the hall and has summoned the newly arrived prisoner Lin Chong for inspection.” Hearing the summons, Lin Chong went before the hall. The commandant said, “You are a newly arrived offender. By an ancient regulation handed down by Emperor Taizu, the Martial and Virtuous, every convict newly entering the camp must receive one hundred initiation strokes. Men, hoist him onto the frame!” Lin Chong pleaded, “I caught a chill on the journey and have not yet recovered. I beg that the beating be postponed.” The squad leader said, “This man is indeed ill at present. I beg you to show him mercy.” The commandant said, “If he truly has an ailment, the punishment may be deferred for now. We shall beat him after he recovers.” The warder said, “The man presently guarding the Hall of the Heavenly King has served there long enough. Lin Chong can be sent to replace him.” The assignment order was endorsed there in the hall. The warder took Lin Chong back to the newcomers’ quarters to collect his baggage, then brought him to the Hall of the Heavenly King to relieve its present guard. The warder said, “Arms Instructor Lin, I have taken excellent care of you. Guarding the Hall of the Heavenly King is the easiest duty in the whole camp. All you need do morning and evening is burn incense and sweep the floor. Look at the other prisoners: they labor from dawn until night and are still given no respite; and those without money or influence are assigned to the underground cells, where they can neither live nor die.” Lin Chong said, “Thank you for taking care of me.” He took out another two or three taels of silver and gave them to the warder, saying, “May I ask you, brother, to see the matter through? It would be better still if you could have the cangue removed from my neck.” The warder accepted the silver and said at once, “Leave it all to me.” He hurried off to report to the commandant, and the cangue was removed as well.

p.src: From then on, Lin Chong made arrangements for sleeping and eating in the Hall of the Heavenly King. Each day he did nothing but burn incense and sweep the floor, and before he knew it forty or fifty days had passed. Having received their bribes, the commandant and the warder grew familiar with him over time. They let him do as he pleased and never came to restrain him. Lord Chai also sent someone to bring him winter clothing and gifts. All the prisoners in the camp also received aid from Lin Chong.

p.src: But let us not belabor the tale. Deep winter was drawing near when, one day around the hour of the Snake, Lin Chong happened to leave the camp for a leisurely stroll. As he walked along, he suddenly heard someone behind him call, “Arms Instructor Lin, how is it that you are here?” Lin Chong turned his head and saw the man. The encounter was to bring Lin Chong within a hair’s breadth of ending his remaining days amid smoke and flame, and to leave him nearly bereft of life upon a road of wind and snow. Who, after all, was the man Lin Chong saw? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
